Brilliant while stretched for four scoreless innings in Game 1, Taylor hasn’t fooled Guardians hitters since and allowed four hits and two walks without recording an out on Thursday night.

Michael Reaves/Getty

Share

This week was supposed to bring the White Sox clinching a postseason series win at home for the first time in 120 years.

“It sucks, you want to do that for the fans,” said second baseman Chase Meidroth after his club’s 9-5 loss to the Guardians in Game 4 of the American League Division Series. “We all wanted it so bad for the fans.”

But behind 18 runs and 17 walks allowed in two games to a Guardians offense that finished 11th in the AL in runs scored, but upgraded at the trade deadline in a way the Sox pitching staff was not, it won’t be happening. Not in this series, and without an about-face in two days, not this year at all.

“Certainly, that’s something that we wanted to give our fans,” said manager Will Venable. “I think we just want to win this series however possible, and wherever that is, we’ll take it.”

It’s fitting that an inter-division battle between Chicago and Cleveland, separated by a game in head-to-head matchups, separated by a game in the AL Central standings, is heading to a final showdown at Progressive Field. At least that’s how a quiet Sox clubhouse is rationalizing two deflating and lopsided losses in front of sold-out crowds.

“I got asked that yesterday and said we turned the page today,” said outfielder Sam Antonacci, asked about turning the page. “We turned the page, but we lost. So, we’ll turn three pages and hopefully win.”

Staff ace Sean Burke walked to the bullpen after the fifth, when the Sox held a brief 4-3 lead and it seemed like he might get the final outs, if Grant Taylor could hold the Guardians at bay. Instead he’ll be available for Game 5; a reason for confidence against a Cleveland team that needed a sixth inning to even register a hit against him in Game 2.

But Taylor did not hold the Guardians at bay, instead allowing all six hitters he faced to reach in a six-run sixth that assured a return to Progressive Field on Saturday. Anthony Kay had begun the inning and retired one of the three hitters he faced. Before him, stalwart rookie Hagen Smith walked the bases loaded and could not complete the first.

“Body felt good, stuff felt good, just didn’t execute,” said Taylor, downplaying workload concerns. “It truly was just execution. I walked two guys and they put the ball in play.”

With Burke at the ready, it’s hard to argue that the White Sox are fully out of pitching, or out of hope for knocking off an 85-win Cleveland team that has taxed their own staff, and asked presumptive Game 5 starter Gavin Williams to get the last three outs of Game 4. But it’s hard to figure what would look different if a Sox postseason pitching plan built on bullpen games was running out of gas.

Erick Fedde had the performances of a lifetime on Thursday, rescuing Smith from his first-inning jam, and keeping the Guardians scoreless until the fifth. A sold-out crowd dressed in black chanted his name in a way the 33-year-old former first-round pick had never previously enjoyed.

“Probably the most surreal moment of my career,” Fedde said. “Hard to put into words.”

Yet when Fedde departed with one out in the fifth, there was still more than half the game to go and not enough Sox arms to navigate it. There were also no answers left for third baseman Jose Ramirez, who looks rejuvenated after homering and driving in three to send the series back to Cleveland.

“Every guy will have their jersey on in the bullpen ready to throw [in Game 5], whether they feel good, whether they feel bad.” Fedde said. “I believe in these guys.”

Inspiring, but also a realistic view of what Sox pitching will be working from at the end of a series that’s stretched them to their limits.
